Normal knee kinematics can be restored to some extent with unicompartmental knee replacement (UKR). While UKR is designed for patients with severe osteoarthritis or significant joint damage, it is still possible to achieve normal knee function and motion in many individuals.

In fact, a study published in the Journal of Arthroplasty found that patients who received a unicompartmental knee replacement preserved their normal knee kinematics compared to those who received a traditional total knee arthroplasty (TKA).

The key factors that influence the success of UKR include:

1. Severity of osteoarthritis: Patients with mild osteoarthritis may be able to achieve good results with UKR, but those with more advanced disease or significant joint damage may require revision surgery.
2. Presence of ligamentous laxity: Patients with anterior laxity of the uninjured knee may experience instability and decreased function after UKR.
3. Knee alignment: Proper alignment is crucial for normal knee kinematics. Patients who receive a metal-backed Onlay tibial component obtained better postoperative mechanical alignment compared to those who received all-polyethylene Inlay prostheses.

While UKR can restore normal knee kinematics, it is essential to discuss the specific requirements and limitations of each patient with their surgeon to determine the best course of treatment.
